The Lagos State Government says it plans to decentralise school inspections across the state’s local council development areas by 2027 to bring education quality assurance officers closer to schools and strengthen monitoring. The Director-General of the Office of Education Quality Assurance, Dr Sulaiman Ogunmuyiwa, disclosed this at a five-day roundtable discussion on education quality assurance in Lagos State, held in Ikeja on Tuesday. Themed “Developing an Efficient Quality Assurance System for Improved Learning Outcomes”, the roundtable gathered education stakeholders, including school owners, teachers, banks and technical partners from Finland and the British High Commission. Ogunmuyiwa said the state was also planning to introduce technology-driven school evaluations, replacing paper-based assessments with digital processes, subject to approval by Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu. “We have 20 zonal offices. Our thinking is that after this roundtable, maybe by next year, we will break down to 57 local council development areas so that our evaluators are closer to the schools that they are supposed to manage,” he said. He added that the proposed digital system had received approval from the Ministry of Innovation, Science and Technology and was awaiting the governor’s approval. We have gone ahead with this to the extent that we are only awaiting the approval of Mr Governor,” Ogunmuyiwa said. He explained that the roundtable was organised to obtain feedback from teachers, school principals, education officials and development partners on existing quality assurance practices and to identify areas for improvement. The director-general also proposed strengthening internal school monitoring by designating vice-principals and assistant head teachers as quality assurance officers, who would liaise directly with his office while remaining within their schools. In his remarks, the Lagos State Commissioner for Basic and Secondary Education, Tolani Alli-Balogun, said education quality assurance must go beyond routine inspections and compliance checks to focus on teaching effectiveness and measurable learning outcomes. “The effectiveness of quality assurance should not be measured solely by the number of schools evaluated or reports generated. It is equally important to recognise that evaluation without appropriate follow-up interventions cannot deliver sustainable improvements,” he said. He added that the five-day engagement should produce practical recommendations, clear institutional responsibilities and a time-bound implementation plan to improve educational standards across the state. Delivering the keynote address, a former Lagos State Commissioner for Budget and Planning, Ben Akabueze, said the focus of education policy should shift from school enrolment to whether pupils were acquiring the knowledge and skills needed to thrive. “The true measure of an education system is not simply the number of classrooms it builds, or the number of students it enrols, as important as these are, but the quality of learning it delivers,” he said. Akabueze called for clearly defined benchmarks for school leadership, teacher performance, curriculum delivery, pupils’ achievement, learning environments and the use of technology. He also advocated regular school self-assessments, lesson observations, teacher professional development and data-driven decision-making, arguing that modern quality assurance should support schools rather than focus solely on identifying faults. “Modern quality assurance is about supporting schools, empowering teachers, strengthening accountability, and creating a culture of continuous improvement,” he said. The Chairperson of the Association of Private Educators in Nigeria, Mrs Lai Koiki, called for fairer, better-publicised school evaluation procedures, stronger advocacy and improved collaboration between public and private schools. She said quality assurance officers should provide support to schools while ensuring that monitoring practices were transparent and consistently applied. “All these children are Lagosians, and they need education. They are Nigerians, and quality assurance should stand at the centre of ensuring improved qualitative education for all children in our schools,” Koiki said.
